title: MCI — Exam 1
description: Core MCI operations: definitions, scene safety, METHANE, START triage and triage tags, incident command and sector officer roles, scene layout and HAZMAT.

questions.text: The word "triage" comes from a French verb meaning:
questions.explanation: From the French "trier" — to sort patients by priority.

questions.text: What turns an incident into a mass casualty incident?
options: The number of casualties overwhelms the local resources available to manage them
An incident that requires air medical transport
A fixed threshold of 25 or more patients
questions.explanation: An MCI is defined by the gap between patient needs and available resources, not by a fixed patient count.

questions.text: Which statement BEST defines a mass casualty incident?
options: There is major loss of community property and revenue
A government has formally declared a disaster area
Healthcare needs exceed the healthcare resources available
The event was caused by an act of terrorism
questions.explanation: Needs exceeding resources is the defining feature; cause and official declarations are irrelevant.

questions.text: An incident whose casualty number or injury severity exceeds the capacity of the first-arriving crews, preventing effective management and transport, is called a:
questions.explanation: Exceeding the capacity of the initial crews defines a multiple casualty incident.

questions.text: A multiple casualty incident is MOST accurately defined as an event in which:
options: Most patients need advanced life support
Mutual aid from other agencies is always required
There are at least 25 patients, more than half critically injured
The number of patients exceeds the resources available to the initial responders
questions.explanation: Again, resources — not a number — define it.

questions.text: An event that overwhelms resources BOTH at the scene AND at the receiving hospitals is the typical definition of a:
questions.explanation: When the whole system — scene and hospitals — is overwhelmed and outside help is required, the event is a disaster.

questions.text: A sudden accident or natural catastrophe that causes great damage or loss of life is a:
questions.explanation: That is the standard definition of a disaster.

questions.text: An event that is expected to lead to an unstable and dangerous situation is described as a:
questions.explanation: A crisis is an unstable, dangerous situation that is developing or expected.

questions.text: The immediate, urgent movement of people away from a threat or actual hazard is called:
questions.explanation: Evacuation is the organised movement of people away from danger.

questions.text: Which of these are examples of natural disasters?
questions.explanation: All three are natural hazards.

questions.text: Which event is MOST likely to produce an open (uncontained) multiple casualty incident?
questions.explanation: A tornado affects a wide, evolving area, so the number and location of victims is not known at the start.

questions.text: When responding to any emergency, whose safety comes first?
questions.explanation: Rescuer safety first — an injured responder becomes another casualty and removes a resource.

questions.text: On arrival at an MCI, your first responsibility is to:
options: Make sure the scene is safe
questions.explanation: Scene safety precedes every other action.

questions.text: As the first crew at an MCI, which action takes priority?
questions.explanation: Size-up comes first; it provides the information for the METHANE report, resource requests and the triage plan.

questions.text: You are a bystander at the scene of an explosion. What should you do first?
options: Enter the scene, then call emergency dispatch
Begin first aid on the injured
Keep curious onlookers away from the scene
Clear debris that may cause injury
questions.explanation: Prevent further casualties (secondary devices, collapse, fire) — don't enter or let others enter.

questions.text: At a building fire, a police officer reports a patient lying in a hallway inside and asks you to help. What is your initial action?
options: Tell the police officer to carry the patient out
Refuse, as it is not your responsibility
Ask fire/rescue to bring the patient out to you
Go in immediately — the patient needs care
questions.explanation: EMS does not enter a fire hazard zone without protective equipment and training; fire/rescue extracts the patient.

questions.text: Why should you approach a driver trapped in a vehicle from the front?
options: So you can check whether the engine is running
So you can reach the ignition key
So the patient does not turn their head to look at you
So you can watch for traffic from behind
questions.explanation: Approaching in the patient's line of sight stops them turning their head, protecting a possibly injured cervical spine.

questions.text: Which patient is the BEST candidate for extrication with a short spinal immobilisation device (e.g., KED)?
options: A walking patient with only minor cuts
A patient already lying on the ground
An unstable (red) patient with suspected spinal injury
A stable, alert patient seated in a vehicle who has neck pain and numbness in the legs
questions.explanation: Short devices are for stable seated patients with suspected spinal injury; unstable patients need rapid extrication.

questions.text: In the METHANE report, N stands for:
questions.explanation: METHANE: Major incident declared, Exact location, Type of incident, Hazards, Access, Number of casualties, Emergency services.

questions.text: In the METHANE report, T stands for:
questions.explanation: T = Type of incident (e.g., road traffic collision, explosion, chemical release).

questions.text: The primary goal of triage at a mass casualty incident is to:
options: Do the most good for the greatest number of potential survivors
Treat and release patients as quickly as possible
Tell hospitals the total number of casualties
Ensure every victim gets immediate medical care
questions.explanation: Triage rations limited resources so the greatest number survive.

questions.text: At an MCI, which victim should you triage first?
questions.explanation: Start where you stand and move systematically — chasing the worst-looking or loudest wastes time.

questions.text: Once the scene is safe, what is the first step of START triage?
options: Direct everyone who can walk to move to a designated area
Apply a triage tag to the nearest patient
Check the respiratory rate of every patient
questions.explanation: START begins with a voice command to identify the walking wounded; the rest are then assessed one by one.

questions.text: The purpose of a voice command at the start of triage is to:
options: Separate out the victims who can walk on their own
Identify the conscious victims for transport
Separate victims by age and sex
questions.explanation: Anyone who can walk to the collection point is initially GREEN.

questions.text: At an MCI, victims are initially grouped according to:
questions.explanation: Ambulatory status is the first sort in START.

questions.text: How long should the initial triage of one patient take?
options: As long as needed for a full assessment
questions.explanation: START is designed to be completed in under a minute per patient.

questions.text: Which interventions are permitted during START triage?
options: Airway, breathing support and IV access
Airway, bleeding control and immediate transport
Open the airway, control major bleeding and position the patient
questions.explanation: Only quick, life-saving actions that take seconds are done during triage.

questions.text: Which is part of managing bleeding during triage?
questions.explanation: During triage you only stop life-threatening haemorrhage (direct pressure or tourniquet) — wound care waits for the treatment area.

questions.text: How are fractures managed during triage?
options: They are not treated during triage
questions.explanation: Splinting and fracture care are done later in the treatment area.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT done during triage?
questions.explanation: None of these are triage interventions; they consume time that should be spent sorting.

questions.text: A patient triaged as GREEN at a disaster scene should be:
options: Told to make their own way to a hospital
Kept at a safe distance from the scene for re-assessment
Told to see their own doctor
questions.explanation: Minor-category patients can deteriorate and must stay in a safe area to be re-triaged.

questions.text: Which findings place a victim in the BLACK (dead/expectant) category?
questions.explanation: Each is an obvious sign of death.

questions.text: During the initial triage phase, a dead body should be moved only to:
options: Let family members view the body
questions.explanation: Bodies are left in place (evidence and identification) unless they block access to the living.

questions.text: Secondary triage should be performed:
questions.explanation: Patients are re-triaged on arrival in the treatment area, where conditions are re-evaluated.

questions.text: As a triage officer, you find an unconscious adult with no obvious injuries who does not breathe after the airway is opened and has no pulse. You should:
options: Tag as expectant (black) and move on
Call one ambulance and load this patient now
Tag as red and make them your priority
questions.explanation: No CPR during MCI triage — resources go to salvageable patients.

questions.text: Which of these patients should be transported first?
options: Apneic patient with a severe head injury
Conscious patient with a fractured femur
questions.explanation: The femur fracture is the most urgent salvageable patient; the apneic head injury is expectant.

questions.text: START stands for:
questions.explanation: START = Simple Triage And Rapid Treatment.

questions.text: In START, RPM stands for:
questions.explanation: The three START parameters.

questions.text: START relies on simple commands and which three physiological parameters?
questions.explanation: Respirations, perfusion (radial pulse/capillary refill) and the ability to follow commands.

questions.text: In RPM, the P (perfusion) is assessed by:
questions.explanation: Capillary refill over 2 seconds or an absent radial pulse = RED.

questions.text: In the START memory aid "30 – 2 – Can do", "Can do" refers to:
questions.explanation: 30 = respiratory rate, 2 = capillary refill seconds, Can do = follows simple commands.

questions.text: A patient who cannot follow simple commands is tagged:
questions.explanation: Failing the mental status check = RED (immediate).

questions.text: A walking man has two amputated fingers and several crushed fingers. He follows commands. His START category is:
questions.explanation: In START anyone who can walk is initially GREEN, however dramatic the injury looks.

questions.text: A 15-year-old with an obviously broken arm is walking around the scene. His category is:
questions.explanation: Ambulatory = GREEN.

questions.text: A responsive 35-year-old man has pale, moist skin and a respiratory rate of 32/min. His category is:
questions.explanation: Respirations over 30/min = RED.

questions.text: An unresponsive man has snoring respirations that improve when you open his airway. His category is:
questions.explanation: Breathing only after airway positioning = RED.

questions.text: A patient who cannot walk is alert, follows commands, breathes 22/min and has a capillary refill under 2 seconds. Using START, they are:
questions.explanation: Non-ambulatory with normal RPM = YELLOW (delayed).

questions.text: A 50-year-old man with bilateral femur fractures cannot walk. He breathes 24/min, has a weak but present radial pulse and follows commands. By strict START criteria he is:
questions.explanation: RR under 30, radial pulse present and obeys commands = YELLOW. Watch closely and re-triage — bilateral femur fractures can cause shock and he may soon become RED.

questions.text: A patient with a severe head injury is not breathing even after the airway is opened. His pulse is 10/min. His category is:
questions.explanation: Apneic after airway repositioning = BLACK in START.

questions.text: What tool do responders use to sort and identify patients during an MCI?
questions.explanation: Triage tags record the priority colour and stay with the patient.

questions.text: Triage tags are mainly used during:
questions.explanation: Tags are an MCI tool for tracking many patients at once.

questions.text: Applying triage tags at the scene is the responsibility of the:
questions.explanation: Initial tagging is done by the triage team under the Triage Officer.

questions.text: On a tear-off triage tag, how do you upgrade a patient to a higher priority?
options: Tear off the lower colour strip so the higher priority shows
Ask the Incident Commander for backup
Write the new priority on the patient's forehead
Discard the old tag and apply a new one
questions.explanation: Tear-off tags are upgraded by removing strips until the correct colour is at the bottom.

questions.text: A tagged patient's condition improves. What should you do with the triage tag?
options: Apply a new tag and keep the original attached
Discard the old tag and apply a new one
questions.explanation: Torn strips cannot be re-attached, so a new tag is applied; keeping the old one preserves the record.

questions.text: Before sending a contaminated patient to hospital, which part of the triage tag must be completed so the receiving hospital can prepare?
questions.explanation: The contamination marking warns the destination so a contaminated patient is not sent to an unprepared facility.

questions.text: In the SLUDGEM mnemonic for nerve-agent poisoning, D stands for:
questions.explanation: SLUDGEM: Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defecation, GI upset, Emesis, Miosis.

questions.text: Which is the only position that is staffed at EVERY incident?
questions.explanation: Every incident, however small, has an Incident Commander.

questions.text: You are on the first ambulance to arrive at an MCI. Which role do you assume?
questions.explanation: The first-arriving crew establishes command until relieved by a more senior officer.

questions.text: Ideally, the first ambulance on scene will be:
options: The last ambulance to leave the scene
The first crew to be relieved
Assigned to transport because it knows the location
The first to transport a red patient
questions.explanation: The first crew takes command and stays to keep continuity until the incident closes.

questions.text: You are Incident Commander when a more senior officer arrives. You should:
options: Send the senior officer to the treatment area
Transfer command and leave with patients
Formally transfer command and stay on to assist
Keep command until the incident ends
questions.explanation: Command is handed over with a briefing; the former IC usually stays as an assistant.

questions.text: During a small incident, the Incident Commander:
options: Delegates all authority to the senior paramedic
Usually does not attend the scene
Acts mainly as the safety officer
May perform all the command functions personally
questions.explanation: ICS is scalable — on a small incident one person can cover every function.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a responsibility of the Incident Commander?
questions.explanation: The IC manages the incident; individual treatment decisions are clinical, not command, functions.

questions.text: The location from which the Incident Commander directs all operations is the:
questions.explanation: The ICP is the on-scene command location.

questions.text: Which ICS role coordinates with other responding agencies?
questions.explanation: The Liaison Officer is the point of contact for other agencies; on small incidents the IC does this personally.

questions.text: In the Gold–Silver–Bronze command structure, Gold is:
questions.explanation: Gold = strategic, Silver = tactical, Bronze = operational.

questions.text: In the Gold–Silver–Bronze command structure, Bronze is:
questions.explanation: Bronze works at the scene, carrying out tasks.

questions.text: Food and clean water are needed for responders during a long MCI. Which ICS section obtains them?
questions.explanation: Logistics provides facilities, services, food and supplies.

questions.text: A news reporter asks you for an interview at an MCI. You should:
options: Tell them to contact your chief executive
Refer them to the Public Information Officer
questions.explanation: All media enquiries go through the Public Information Officer.

questions.text: A backup ambulance arriving at an established MCI should report to the:
questions.explanation: Arriving units check in at staging and wait to be assigned, so the IC knows what resources are on scene.

questions.text: Which sector officer sorts and prioritises all victims?
questions.explanation: Sorting is triage.

questions.text: Which officer tells dispatch and the hospitals where each patient is being sent?
questions.explanation: The Transport Officer coordinates destinations with dispatch and hospitals.

questions.text: Which officer records each patient's destination and tracking number?
questions.explanation: Transport keeps the log of which patient went where.

questions.text: The Staging Officer is responsible for:
options: Making sure every patient has been triaged
Confirming that patients have been transported
Telling the Treatment Officer when to transport patients
Reporting the status of available resources to the Incident Commander
questions.explanation: Staging manages and reports on incoming resources until they are assigned.

questions.text: Which officer monitors operations to make sure responders follow safety procedures?
questions.explanation: The Safety Officer watches for hazards and unsafe practices.

questions.text: Who gives the Incident Commander a risk assessment of the incident action plan?
questions.explanation: Risk assessment is a core Safety Officer function.

questions.text: Who has the authority to stop a rescuer immediately if they are in danger?
questions.explanation: The Safety Officer can halt unsafe acts on the spot.

questions.text: What is gathered in the staging area?
options: Supplies and members of the media
questions.explanation: Staging holds incoming resources until they are assigned.

questions.text: Patients are cared for in which area of an MCI?
questions.explanation: Self-explanatory.

questions.text: A team of physicians arrives at an MCI from a local hospital. Where are they best used?
questions.explanation: Physicians add the most value giving advanced care in the treatment area.

questions.text: Which colour tarp in the treatment area should be closest to the loading/transport area?
questions.explanation: RED patients leave first, so their tarp sits nearest the ambulance loading point.

questions.text: HAZMAT is short for:
questions.explanation: HAZardous MATerials.

questions.text: A substance that can harm life, property or the environment is called a:
questions.explanation: That is the definition of a hazardous material.

questions.text: Signs on a transport vehicle that identify the hazardous material it is carrying are called:
questions.explanation: Placards show the hazard class and UN number on the outside of vehicles.

questions.text: How can a hazardous material enter the body?
questions.explanation: All four routes of exposure apply.

questions.text: At a hazardous materials incident, EMS should stage in the:
questions.explanation: EMS stages and treats in the cold (support) zone, upwind and uphill.

questions.text: At a HAZMAT incident, contaminated patients must be decontaminated:
options: After they are treated at the scene
Before they enter the treatment area
When they arrive at the hospital
questions.explanation: Decontamination happens in the warm zone before patients reach the clean treatment area. Quick initial triage may be done before decontamination to set its order.

questions.text: Which is NOT a role of the first-arriving EMT at a possible hazardous materials emergency?
options: Rescuing victims still in the spill area
Recognising that it is a hazardous materials emergency
questions.explanation: Entering the hot zone is for trained, protected HAZMAT teams only.
